title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
description: While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into gr
body: While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism."While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said."We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic"."There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

schema.headline: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
description: A British stuntman and actor is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II, saying he suffered "excruciating" burns and permanent scarring in an a
body: A British stuntman and actor is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II, saying he suffered "excruciating" burns and permanent scarring in an accident while filming a scene on a burning ship.Edward Sarsfield was playing a dead soldier in the movie in 2023 when a gas line used for special effects exploded on the vessel, causing 20ft flames that made his costume catch fire, his legal claim said.He "panicked and ran" before colleagues threw bottles of water over his burns, which covered about 15% of his body, including his face, his arms and hands, he said.Sarsfield is suing August Street Films, whose defence said it admits liability for the accident, but has not made an admission about the alleged injuries or agreed to the requested £200,000 damages.Gladiator II, released in 2024, was the long-awaited sequel to the hit 2000 drama starring Russell Crowe. The follow-up was directed by Sir Ridley Scott and starred Paul Mescal and Denzel Washington.Sarsfield, 47, from Liverpool, said he was working as an extra in a scene in Morocco in which a coastal castle was under siege from an approaching ship."The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court."He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards."He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms."He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh."He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital."Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries."The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment."The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

schema.headline: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion

title: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots in Morriston
description: Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.South Wales Police said a vehicle on the
body: Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday.A 41-year-old man from Llansamlet, Swansea, had been arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life, while a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, had been arrested on suspicion of affray.The force said officers were still investigating and that it had been declared a critical incident.Residents have been told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display, have been cancelled.Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appears to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.South Wales Police said the incident was ongoing, with road closures in place.Ch Supt Stephen Jones said: "A policing presence will be visible in the area whilst this investigation is ongoing.""It is important that people avoid the area so we can effectively deal with this incident and return the area to normality."The local football club, Morriston Town AFC, cancelled a planned firework display on Friday."Unfortunately, the police have advised due to an issue ongoing, the event has to be cancelled. With immediate effect," it said in a social media post, advising people to stay at home.

schema.headline: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots in Morriston

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time. His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here."It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand. On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims. "As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

schema.headline: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand

title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Dona
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests."Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."Figure caption, Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.Figure caption, What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?Miller's hardline views sets up clash with CongressWhile Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans."Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X.  "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.Image source, Getty ImagesOn Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises."Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle

title: Coventry City: Frank Lampard questions decisions after Sky Blues fall at Everton
description: Coventry boss Frank Lampard questioned why his side were not given a penalty after a trio of decisions went against them in defeat at Everton.Thierno
body: Coventry boss Frank Lampard questioned why his side were not given a penalty after a trio of decisions went against them in defeat at Everton.Thierno Barry's double and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's late goal helped the hosts come from behind to win 3-1 on Friday.Yann Gboho gave Coventry the lead after the break, yet the visitors felt they should have had a first-half spot-kick.James Tarkowski tugged Caleb Yirenkyi's hair while jumping for a ball, with referee Stuart Attwell dismissing the Sky Blues' claims.The rules have been relaxed around hair pulling this season and it does not automatically mean a foul or a red card, with excessive force and intent also being taken into consideration - but former Everton boss Lampard believes the officials got it wrong.He said: "They're saying it's not enough of a pull and I think it's a hard area to be in. What is a hair pull? You've decided it is but it's not enough."I have looked at them, sometimes with emotions in the moment you can't be clear on the sidelines. "I think the rules are fine. It's not a red card. I kind of get that because I think in a game of football there's a lot of stuff happens that's not absolutely dramatic. "You know they can happen but I think if the the rule remains that it's a foul so I felt it was a foul."Lampard also felt Taiwo Awoniyi was fouled by Vitalii Mykolenko before Coventry went ahead, although replays showed it was outside the box, and Barry handled the ball before his second goal - although video assistant referee (VAR) Timothy Wood ruled it was not a handball offence."Taiwo for me on the line of the box is a penalty. You've got to give the foul in real time anyway, the ref did let it go, and I felt it was a penalty," Lampard added, with defeat leaving Coventry 16th in the Premier League."The Barry one is handball, I've heard they are saying it didn't touch his hand but I've seen an angle where he has flicked it in with the final touch. VAR is there for that."I can't sit here and say I know everything and they should give all three of them, if one or two of them don't go our way, but they would clearly change the game."Everton boss David Moyes denied Barry handled the ball and also felt the hair pulling rule needs addressing. After his team moved fifth, the Scot said: "We've had plenty [of decisions] which have gone against us. It certainly doesn't hit his hand."The hair pull rule has changed so it would be a booking if it was but I still think it's ridiculous that rule is in the game. I can't understand why they don't fix this completely because I don't see it as a good rule at all." Three big VAR calls, and they all went against Coventry. Lampard must have walked under a ladder earlier today.There is a strong argument that the Sky Blues should have been awarded a penalty for the Tarkowski hair pullThe law was relaxed at the start of this season to say not all hair pulling should be a red card, after three players were sent off last season.The idea is that not all contact with the hair should be an offence, and it needs to be an act with excessive force for a player to be sent off.But, for a penalty, the actions of Tarkowski only need to be a foul, not violent conduct. If accidental, it should not be a spot-kick.Did the Wood, the VAR, concentrate too much on a possible handball by Tarkowski within the move?It looked like there was a movement of Tarkowski's arm to pull the hair which should have led to a VAR intervention. Coventry probably should have received a penalty.Then early in the second half came a possible penalty as Mykolenko clipped Awoniyi.The camera positioned level with the edge of the penalty area did seem to show the contact was outside the area, and the VAR cannot intervene to award a free-kick.It might have been a soft VAR intervention even if the potential foul was inside the box.Perhaps most controversially was Barry's second goal, with the ball appearing to touch the striker's arm before it went into the goal.We have seen this kind of situation a few times this season, most notably when Nottingham Forest had a goal against Tottenham disallowed.This time, the VAR decided he did not have the necessary conclusive proof to be sure the ball touched the hand.Yet it does seem like there is a change of direction after Barry's hand touches the ball, and that was the reason it goes into the goal. It looked like handball should have been given on video review although others might argue that ruling it out would have been too forensic.Three decisions, and Coventry can feel aggrieved about two of them.

schema.headline: Coventry City: Frank Lampard questions decisions after Sky Blues fall at Everton

title: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans
description: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everythin
body: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off." The next day he went for a walk."[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong."It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded. For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event. At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours. "We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.The much talked about "Be Prepared" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan. Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio. It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online., external They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack."It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population. However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis. "When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.  We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails. In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications". However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour. The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.The response from the government was that while  copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused."If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.It felt like an omen.

schema.headline: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans

title: 'My mortgage has gone up already': How rising interest rates are hitting people's pockets
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected by rising interest rates ByDaniel Thomas and Rapha
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected by rising interest rates ByDaniel Thomas and Raphael SheridanBBC NewsOn Thursday, the Bank of England increased interest rates for the first time in over three years as it tries to get a grip on rising inflation linked to the Iran war. Experts say there could be more hikes over the next 18 months, as the conflict continues to push up food, fuel and energy prices across the UK and worldwide. Higher interest rates affect borrowing costs, however, which means mortgages, credit cards and personal loans could get more expensive for millions, even as savings rates improve. For some, it could mean extra financial pressure at a time when they are already struggling with the cost of living. The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected.'Our tracker mortgage will go up'Image source, Peter GillImage caption, Peter Gill says his family's costs are risingPeter Gill, 48, is one of the around 1.3 million Britons on a variable rate mortgage.These loans track the Bank of England base rate, with a margin on top determined by the lender, so any rise in interest rates can push up repayments. Peter, who runs a small tiling business in Halifax, says his monthly repayments will go up by roughly £45 following Thursday's quarter-percentage point increase and he's worried they could climb higher.But he still thinks it'd be more expensive to move onto a fixed-rate deal - which is when you pay a set amount of monthly interest for a period - and is prepared to stay put for now. Figure caption, Watch: What does the raise in interest rates mean?His higher mortgage costs come as the "cost of everything is going up", he says. The father of two, who has a combined household income of £45,000 with his wife Faye, is having to pay his staff more because of increases in the national minimum wage. Raw material costs have also risen due to the war in Iran. At home, the family's food, gas and electricity bills have gone up and he says he's working "about six and a half days a week" to shield them from the worst of it."From my point of view, inflation goes up which costs you, then interest rates go up and you have even less money."  'My mortgage is going up by £200 a month'Image source, Ben Schofield/BBCImage caption, Dawn Fazackerley-King is struggling but says there's "no more fat to trim"Most UK mortgage holders are on fixed-rate deals, but that doesn't necessarily protect them when the Bank of England puts up rates. David Hollingworth, from brokers L&C Mortgages, says many people will be shocked at how much higher fixed-rate deals are than they were five years ago following recent increases."Fixed rates have already risen due to market anticipation that interest rates would need to rise to combat higher inflation," he says.Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother of two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month."I don't know where that money is going to come from, it's something we are going to have to figure out as a family. It's stressful."She and her husband, who have a joint income of about £70,000, have already gone through their direct debits and there's "no more obvious fat to trim".There is also no scope for them to take on additional work, as they both work full time."We're still living in the same property, our household costs are remaining the same," Dawn says. "It's an additional cost of several hundred pounds but we're not getting anything extra for that." 'My credit card repayments could rise'Image source, Ben ThomasImage caption, Higher interest rates are "another cost to deal with", says BenWhen the Bank of England increases its base rate, credit card borrowing costs also tend to increase, although the impact is not always immediate.It may affect people with outstanding debts, as providers can increase the interest rates they charge with 30 days' notice.  Ben Thomas, 41, from Shropshire, ditched his career as a chartered accountant during the Covid pandemic after a mental health crisis and retrained as a paramedic. But the drop in income left him reliant on credit cards and personal loans for everyday living expenses and he is now £52,000 in debt.Ben says he's reached an agreement to pause the interest on most of it, but he is still incurring charges on around £2,000 of credit card debt and is worried about his repayments going up. "With all that's going on, rising interest rates is another cost to deal with," he tells the BBC.As well as overall debt repayments of around £300 a month, he and his wife pay £760 on their mortgage. They have also struggled with higher food and energy bills.Simon Trevethick is head of communications at StepChange, which has been helping Ben manage his debt. He says the debt charity has seen a 20% increase in people asking for support this year and warned of tougher times ahead."If higher borrowing costs feed through into household budgets over the coming months, we could see further pressure on people seeking support."

schema.headline: 'My mortgage has gone up already': How rising interest rates are hitting people's pockets

title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
description: Image source, Jo Hale/Getty ImagesImage caption, Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assaultByCulture and m
body: Image source, Jo Hale/Getty ImagesImage caption, Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assaultByCulture and media editorWarning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual actsNo British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.His life has been one long personal rebrand.He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.Image source, Frank Micelotta/Getty Images for MTVImage caption, Brand performing at the MTV Video Music Awards a year after his memoir was publishedBrand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies. He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.An era that celebrated casual sexismImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Back then lads' magazines ruled - with their covers and double page spreads full of topless glamour models and half-naked female celebritiesThe late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it. In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise."There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking."I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."Image source, Jo Hale/Getty ImagesImage caption, My Booky Wook topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook."I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.Fame and success brought him 'birds' "The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".Image source, Don Arnold/WireImageImage caption, Meeting crowds backstage in Sydney in 2010 In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that."The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times"."It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.'Brand was enabled'Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it"."People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on"."Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."We now understand quite how terrible.

schema.headline: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight

title: Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja claims whole Australia team knew about use of sandpaper to tamper with ball against South Africa
description: Usman Khawaja has claimed the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball in the final Test of their 2018 series wit
body: Usman Khawaja has claimed the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball in the final Test of their 2018 series with South Africa.In extracts of his autobiography - Sabr - published in the Sydney Morning Herald,, external the former opening batter said Australia had also used the ball-tampering tactic in the Test before the infamous match in Cape Town.The incident - nicknamed 'sandpapergate' - was widely condemned and led to bans for captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft."It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja, 39, told the Sydney Morning Herald.The four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including current Test captain Pat Cummins, have consistently denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan.In 2021, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement saying they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".Khawaja, who scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests, said that discussions about tampering with the ball began during the second Test of the series against South Africa.That match, played at Port Elizabeth - now Gqeberha - led to what Khawaja said was the "discovery of sandpaper as an effective agent" after "open" discussions held in the dressing room at St George's Park."At this point Smith essentially threw his hands in the air and said he didn't want to know," Khawaja wrote.Australia were rumbled in the third Test when television cameras clearly showed Bancroft using sandpaper on the ball to help generate reverse swing.Khawaja was also shocked not to be asked to provide any evidence during Cricket Australia's investigation."In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth," he said."The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."While Smith, Warner and Bancroft - all batters - were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."Days after Bancroft's interview was published, the quartet released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again."We did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands."And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage."We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."Before Australia's recent Test series in South Africa - which the Proteas won 2-1 - Cummins said he had spoken to Khawaja about the publication of the book.The 33-year-old said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations and felt it was "all dealt with then" and the team had "moved on"."He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries," Cummins said on 8 October."Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times."Khawaja also said he had consistently argued that the team should take responsibility together, including in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test.He wrote: "I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified."In his memoir, named after an Arabic term for resilience and endurance, Khawaja dedicated the chapter on Cape Town to Smith, Warner and Bancroft.The left-handed batter said he thought the trio "deserve" the "justice" of collective blame from the team as a whole.He added: "None of those three want to be the first to say anything. And rightly so, it will just be hearsay and 'their word' if they do. They needed someone else to say something."But I'm not doing this for any other reason than I think it's the right thing to do."

schema.headline: Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja claims whole Australia team knew about use of sandpaper to tamper with ball against South Africa

title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.Markle w
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies". Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring. No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest. FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle. "Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said. He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide". Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country. Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr. Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr. The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter. In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material

title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
description: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in
body: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself"."Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media  meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.The actor and comedian denied the allegations. On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand. Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry. Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

schema.headline: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist

title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
description: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private bus
body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President."Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.

schema.headline: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested

title: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
description: Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.The Canadian stand-up and T
body: Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentary interview with Louis Theroux that there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain."They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief."Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened."I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.Ryan continued on the podcast: "This verdict came because women were hurt, and I worry as well about what happens next."Because he's obviously spent a long time cultivating this idea that the establishment have invented these claims against him, and he's martyred himself to a growing audience who really still think that it is the courageous survivors who are the villains in this story."Ryan's comments came on the same day that former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey questioned how and why Brand was able to "get away with it so long?"Why didn't anybody intervene? Why did those around him enable him? Why didn't any of the senior executives who worked with him call time?" she said on BBC Radio 5 Live's Nick Campbell on Friday."I think they were partly mesmerised. I think he seemed to be 'cool' for a while. I think he did have charisma," added Heggessey."He brought in a young audience, which a lot of broadcasters crave. So I think all of those reasons... and as people have said, he did hide in plain sight."Bear Grylls, the adventurer and host of the Discovery Channel's show Man Vs Wild, has spoken about when he helped baptise Brand in the River Thames in 2024. "Brand's faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism," he said on X, adding that he had attended a few baptisms, including "visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes". Grylls said he attended as part of a calling of his faith "to love and serve anyone", adding it is "the sick who need healing". "Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn't want to ever discourage someone's coming to faith," he continued. But, he said, it was “right that justice has now been served."I can't imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day."Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.The actor and comedian denied the allegations.None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction."One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated."There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate."The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

schema.headline: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
